situations.title: The client changes requirements 2 weeks before release
situations.summary: A client asks for a change late in the project. Enter your real numbers, compare accepting, deferring and declining, then produce a Change Request you can send.

questions.label: What is the change, in one line?
questions.placeholder: Add CSV export to the reports screen

questions.label: What exactly does the client want?
questions.help: Ask the client for specifics: which screens or deliverables, what is the acceptance criterion, what happens if it is not there.

questions.label: How critical is it for the client?
questions.help: Ask: what happens to them if this is not in this release?

options.label: Must-have (blocks their launch, legal or contractual)
Important (hurts, but they can launch without it)

questions.label: Average cost per person-day (USD)
questions.help: Use the internal blended rate or your best estimate.

questions.label: Estimated effort for the change (person-days)
questions.help: Ask the team for a quick estimate. Do not guess alone.

questions.label: Schedule buffer left before the release (working days)
Share of the change cost the client will pay (%)
questions.help: 0 if the contract does not allow billing the change.

questions.label: Contract penalty per day of delay (USD, optional)
Testing and coordination overhead (%)
questions.help: Extra effort on top of the raw estimate for QA, regression, docs and meetings.

questions.label: Share of the work that can be split across the team (%)
questions.help: Not all work can be shared. 100 means perfectly splittable.

questions.label: Productive share of a working day (%)

accept.label: Accept the change
nextSteps: Send the Change Request to the client and get written approval before any work starts.
Tell the team what is changing and re-baseline the plan together.
Update the schedule, budget and risk register.
Agree on a freeze: no further changes without a new Change Request.

defer.label: Defer to the next release
nextSteps: Offer the client a dated slot in the next release, not an open-ended promise.
Write the change into the backlog with the agreed priority.
Explain what the client gets on time instead.
Confirm with the client in writing.

decline.label: Decline the change
nextSteps: Prepare the reason in the client's terms: dates and money, not 'we are busy'.
Offer an alternative such as a smaller version or a workaround.
Raise it with your manager before the call if the client is senior.
Record the decision and the reason.

pitfalls: Saying yes in the meeting before anyone has estimated the change.
Ignoring the testing and coordination effort that comes with every change.
Absorbing the cost silently, so the client never sees what each change costs.
Telling the client about the delay after the date has already slipped.
Declining without offering a deferred or smaller alternative.

reflectionPrompts.label: What did you learn from comparing the options?
What would you do differently next time?
